overview: Tenochtitlan brought canals, markets, workshops and ceremonial architecture into a large lake city. This card focuses on the capital's civic and artistic life within the Aztec imperial world.

items.text: Canals and raised causeways connected the capital to surrounding lakeshore towns. Canoes carried people and goods through the urban network.
Aqueducts supplied fresh water, while neighborhood communities maintained local temples and markets.
Stone carvers used stone and hardwood tools, fiber cords, water and sand to shape even hard materials into detailed sculpture.
The Templo Mayor paired shrines to Tlaloc and Huitzilopochtli. Successive rulers enlarged the complex, sometimes also responding to flooding and unstable ground.
The capital's markets offered food and luxury goods. Its neighborhoods included potters, weavers, sculptors, lapidaries and featherworkers.

fall.text: Tenochtitlan fell in 1521. Spanish rulers built a new colonial capital over the devastated city.
